summary: This unit teaches you to plan and manage a conference from first idea to final report: agreeing aims and a planning structure, building and controlling a budget and setting the delegate fee, choosing a venue and checking its contract, designing the programme and looking after speakers, marketing and registration, planning catering, transport and access, managing risk and safety, running the event on the day, and evaluating and reporting. It is written for supervisors and managers who organise conferences for Jamaican associations, businesses, schools and public bodies.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. A **conference** is a planned gathering of many delegates, often from several organisations, who follow a programme of talks, workshops and networking over one or more days. A conference is not an ordinary meeting: it needs a committee, a budget that depends on how many people pay to attend, a venue contract, speakers, suppliers, registration, health and safety planning, and a final report.

In Jamaica, conferences are organised by professional and trade associations, ministries and agencies, schools and colleges, churches, non-governmental organisations and businesses, often at hotels in Kingston, Montego Bay, Ocho Rios and Negril, or at university and conference centres. This unit covers the work of the **conference manager**: the person who turns an idea into a safe, well-run, financially sound event.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario questions and sums (break-even, contingency, room blocks, percentages).
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as plenary, attrition, MICE) and longer planning answers.
**Group practical tasks**: a one-day conference plan with budget, programme and risk register, and a simulated conference morning with incidents and an evaluation. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and always round **up** when you count people or rooms. You cannot have 128.6 delegates.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Start with purpose, audience and aims

blocks.p: Before venues or speakers, agree **why** the conference is being held, **who** it is for and **what it must achieve**. Write aims that can be measured: '250 paying delegates', 'an average satisfaction score of at least 4 out of 5', 'a surplus of J$200,000', 'three new member benefits agreed'. Without measurable aims you cannot judge success at the end.

head: Feature
Ordinary meeting
Conference
rows: A planned programme: plenaries, breakouts, workshops, breaks, social events
Usually part of a normal budget
Often its own budget; delegates pay fees; sponsors and exhibitors
Months to a year or more

blocks.p: A **steering committee** (or organising committee) makes the main decisions. **Sub-committees** or working groups do the detail, for example programme, sponsorship, marketing and registration, logistics and venue, finance. Give each one **written terms of reference**: its tasks, limits, budget, who it reports to and when. Then each group knows what it must do, and what it may not decide on its own.

head: When (for a conference about 8 to 12 months ahead)
Main tasks
rows: Agree aims, committees and budget outline; choose date and venue (large venues book early); set the theme
Sign venue contract; confirm keynote speakers; open sponsorship and exhibitor sales; launch the website; announce the date
Open registration with an early-bird rate; confirm programme; arrange transport, accommodation, catering, insurance; marketing push
Close early-bird; confirm numbers; finalise speaker briefs; print materials; recruit and brief volunteers; check risk register
Final numbers to venue and caterer; run sheet; technical checks; briefings; badges; walk-through
Run the event; evaluate; pay suppliers; close finances; report; thank people; follow up

blocks.note: For a 500-delegate conference in Montego Bay, planning often starts twelve months ahead. The date and the place shape every other plan, and large venues are scarce at peak times.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Conference manager / project lead**: aims, timeline, who does what, decisions.
**Finance officer**: budget, income, payments, reports.
**Programme planner**: sessions, speakers, timings.
**Venue and logistics officer**: venue, catering, transport, accommodation, access.
**Marketing and registration officer**: promotion, website, delegate list.
**Risk and safety officer**: register, plans, insurance, safety.
**Volunteer and delegate-care coordinator**.

blocks.p: Hold regular meetings with a short agenda, keep **minutes with actions, owners and dates**, and keep one master plan that everyone can see.

head: Type
What it is
Examples
rows: Do not change with the number of delegates
Venue hire, audio-visual equipment, speakers' fees and travel, marketing, insurance, signage, event staff
Lunches and coffee breaks, conference bags, printed materials, name badges, certificates, transport per person

blocks.p: Get **written quotes** for all main items. Show GCT, service charges and any other charges, at the rates that apply when you sign. List **income**: delegate fees, sponsorship, exhibitor stands, grants, other sales.

Add a **contingency** (often 5% to 10% of total costs) for things you cannot foresee. If the budget totals J$5,600,000 and the committee sets 10%, hold J$560,000 back. Use it only with the committee's approval and record the reason.
The **break-even number** is the number of paying delegates at which income equals costs.
**Break-even = fixed costs ÷ (fee − variable cost per delegate).** The part in brackets is the **contribution** each delegate makes towards fixed costs.

**Example:** fixed costs J$2,400,000. Each delegate costs J$9,000 in meals and materials, and the fee is J$25,000. Contribution = 25,000 − 9,000 = J$16,000. Break-even = 2,400,000 ÷ 16,000 = **150 delegates**. If the answer is not a whole number, round **up**: 128.6 means 129 delegates. Check: 150 × 25,000 = 3,750,000 income; costs 2,400,000 + 150 × 9,000 = 3,750,000.

flow: List all costs at the expected number of delegates and add the contingency
Subtract sponsorship and other income
Divide what remains by the expected number of paying delegates, and add the surplus you want
Compare with similar conferences and with what your members can pay
Set early-bird, member, student and group rates with clear closing dates
Test the break-even number: is it realistic to reach it?

blocks.p: **Example:** costs at 120 delegates are J$2,520,000, plus 10% contingency (J$252,000) = J$2,772,000. With no sponsorship the fee that just covers this is 2,772,000 ÷ 120 = **J$23,100**. A fee with a small surplus would be higher. If sponsors give J$600,000, the amount to be raised from fees falls to J$2,172,000, or J$18,100 per delegate.

A sponsor may give cash or goods in return for recognition: a logo, a speaking slot, a stand. Before accepting, check that the sponsor **fits the aims**, agree the benefits **in writing**, and look for **conflicts of interest**. In a public body, do not let a sponsor who has business with the body gain any advantage in decisions. Give exhibitors a **pack**: floor plan, set-up times, rules, power, insurance and contacts.

An **early-bird rate** (for example 15% off if paid by a set date: J$20,000 becomes J$17,000) brings in cash and firm numbers early, when you must pay deposits. Plan a **cash flow**: when money comes in and when large payments fall due, so that you are never unable to pay a deposit.

ul: Update the budget monthly: **committed, actual and forecast**.
If a cost is forecast to be J$400,000 over (for example catering), **find the cause, seek savings or approval, and update the forecast**.
Keep all quotes, orders, invoices and approvals.
After the event, **check invoices, pay suppliers and compare actual with budget**.

blocks.note: Never agree a cost or sign a contract that exceeds your authority. Follow the procurement rules if you work for a public body, and **record why** each supplier was chosen.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Question
What to check
rows: Main hall capacity in the layouts you need; breakout rooms; foyer for registration and exhibitors; a room for speakers and for the team
Step-free routes, accessible toilets, lifts, parking, transport links, distance from airports and hotels
Enough rooms, rates, whether a room block is offered, nearby alternatives for a residential conference
Sound, screens, projectors, internet speed, power, backup generator, technicians
Menus, dietary needs, kitchen capacity, serving points
Total price including GCT and service charge; what is included; deposits
References, fire exits, licences, safe capacity, emergency plan

blocks.p: Compare venues in a **scoring table** against the criteria that matter most to the aims, weighting the important ones. Choose the venue that has **the rooms, space and access needed**, not just the lowest price.

Before signing, **visit the site** with the sub-committee. Check that rooms, access, sound, internet and services match what the venue promised. Walk the route a delegate takes from arrival to the main hall. Look for pillars that block views, poor sound, noise from next door, narrow doors and distant toilets. Note what the venue promises and get it **in writing** in the contract.

head: Layout
Description
Best for
rows: Rows of chairs facing the stage, no tables
Rows of tables with chairs facing the front
Round tables with chairs on one side, facing the stage
Workshops and group work where people also see the stage and screen
Tables arranged for a small group
Round tables with chairs all round

blocks.h: Key clauses in a venue contract

head: Clause or term
What it means
What to check
rows: Exactly what space is booked, for when, including set-up and take-down
What is included, deposit dates and amounts, how GCT and service charges are shown
Written quote totals match the contract
A block of rooms held for your delegates; attrition lets you take a stated percentage fewer without charge
Percentage allowed, dates for releasing rooms, charge for unused rooms
The final number of meals you must give the venue (often 72 hours before). You pay for at least that number, even if fewer attend
Deadline, minimum, how extra meals are charged
What you pay if you cancel at different dates before the event (usually a sliding scale)
Frees both sides when events outside their control, such as a hurricane, make the event impossible
What events are included; refunds or credits
What the venue provides and what you must bring or hire
Who insures what; liability for damage or injury
Fire exits, capacity, security, accessible facilities
Written safe capacity for each room

blocks.p: **Example (room block):** a hotel holds 80 rooms for two nights at J$18,000 a night, and allows the group to fall 20% below the block without charge. The minimum is 80 × 0.80 = 64 rooms. If only 55 are used, the group is 9 rooms short, and owes 9 × 2 × 18,000 = **J$324,000**. If a hotel allows a 10% drop below 120 rooms, the lowest number without penalty is 120 × 0.90 = 108.

blocks.note: Read every contract line by line. Ask someone with authority (and legal advice where available) to sign. Never rely on a promise made only in conversation.
blocks.label: Safety

terms: Plenary
A session that all delegates attend together, often in the main hall.
Keynote
The main speaker, who opens the conference or a day with a talk that sets the theme.
Breakout session
A smaller session on a narrower topic, held alongside others so that delegates can choose.
Workshop
A hands-on session in which delegates work in groups.
Panel
A discussion among several speakers with a chair.
Networking
Planned time and space for delegates to meet each other.

flow: Start from the aims and the delegates' needs (use a survey of members and last year's evaluation)
Open each day with a strong plenary or keynote, then add breakout sessions on narrower topics
Mix talks with discussion and workshops so that delegates do not only listen
Build in **breaks, meals and networking time** (a programme with no time to meet people is a common complaint)
Allow time for moving between rooms and for sessions that run late
End with a closing plenary that sums up and states what happens next
Test the programme against the aims: does every session serve one?

ul: For a workshop where 120 delegates must work in groups and still see the stage and screen, use **cabaret** layout.
If each breakout room holds 60 and three sessions run at once, ask delegates to **choose at registration** and set a limit per session, with a reserve list.
Offer a variety of voices: local and regional experts, different sectors, women and men, new and experienced speakers.

flow: Select speakers who match the aims and the audience (knowledge, speaking skill, reputation)
Invite in writing: topic, length, audience, date, fee and expenses offered
Confirm **in writing**: topic, timing, fee, travel and accommodation, slide deadline, equipment needed
Send a briefing pack: programme, room, layout, audience, timing, contact on the day
Collect slides early and check them
Look after the speaker on the day: greeting, green room, technical check, water, a host
Thank in writing, share evaluation results, pay promptly

blocks.p: For overseas speakers (for example from Trinidad), also arrange travel, **invitation letters for visas** where needed, airport transfer, accommodation and local contact. Have a **back-up plan** (a back-up speaker or a prepared panel) in case a speaker cannot come.

Give each session chair a **written brief**: timing, speaker details and introductions, how to handle questions, how to signal time, and what to do if a speaker is absent or runs over. A good chair keeps the programme to time, so that later speakers and breaks are not squeezed.

ul: Collect slides before the event; load them onto one computer.
Hold a **technical rehearsal** the day before with the technician.
Take a **backup copy** on a flash drive, and keep a spare laptop and adaptors.
Check sound, microphones, screens, internet and power in every room.
Know who to call if equipment fails.

head: Format
Strengths
Limits
rows: Best networking and attention; builds relationships
Highest cost (travel, hotel, venue); some people cannot travel
Low cost; large reach; no travel
Weaker networking; screen fatigue; needs stable internet and good hosts
Needs sound, cameras, a stable link and a **host who brings online delegates in**; costs more than online only

ul: State the **benefit** to the delegate, not just the date and place.
Use the channels your audience uses: association e-mail lists, social media, website, WhatsApp groups, newsletters, partner organisations, radio.
Keep a schedule of messages: announcement, early-bird deadline, speaker news, last chance.
If registrations are low six weeks out, **find out why**: check the message, the channels, the price and the timing, then act.
Use an **online registration form** and payment, with a confirmation message and a receipt showing GCT where it applies.
Ask about **dietary needs and access needs**, so you can plan catering and accessibility.
Keep a delegate list that is **accurate and secure**.
Plan for **no-shows**: delegates who register but neither attend nor cancel. Keep a cancellation policy and plan numbers using past patterns.

blocks.p: Registration forms hold names, phone numbers, employers and sometimes medical notes. The general aims of the data protection law: **collect only what is needed, use it for the event, keep it secure and keep it no longer than needed**. Tell delegates how their data will be used. Do not share the list with sponsors without consent.

ul: Plan **meals, coffee breaks and water** for the numbers in the guarantee.
Include vegetarian, vegan, halal, gluten-free and other needs: for example, 12.5% of 320 delegates need gluten-free lunches, which is 40 meals; 15% of 240 vegetarian is 36.
Check the caterer's food safety and handling.
Plan serving points so queues are short.
For delegates in several hotels, book enough **buses with set pick-up times** and a contact for each.
Give delegates a clear map, parking information and the address.
Arrange airport transfers for overseas delegates.
Consider a **room block** with a booking code.
Check **step-free access** to rooms, toilets, stage and transport.
Ask in registration what delegates need: sign language interpreters, a hearing loop, large print, quiet space, reserved seating.
Make sure the speakers' slides are clear and accessible, with captions or transcripts for online sessions.
Provide for delegates from other Caribbean countries and from Africa: visas, translation where needed, food, prayer or quiet rooms.

blocks.p: Volunteers (for example college students) help at registration, in rooms and with directions. **Brief them before the conference** on tasks, contacts, the programme, emergencies, and who is in charge. Give them a break and thank them. Do not leave a volunteer alone to deal with an emergency.

sections.title: Risk, health and safety, and insurance

blocks.p: A **risk register** lists everything that could go wrong, and for each: its **likelihood**, its **impact**, the **controls** (what you will do to prevent or reduce it) and the **owner**. A simple score: likelihood (1 to 5) × impact (1 to 5). A score of 20 or more needs the most attention.

head: Risk
Likelihood
Impact
Controls (examples)
rows: Hurricane or severe weather near the date
Choose dates with care; agree a decision date and communication plan with venue, caterer and insurer; consider cancellation or postponement terms and online back-up
Generator at venue; backup internet; printed programme; offline copy of slides
Marketing plan, early checks at 12, 8 and 6 weeks, flexible costs, break-even test
Back-up speaker or panel; recorded session
Written safe capacity for each room; stop registrations or use overflow with screens
Clear exits, marshals, briefed team and assembly point
Reliable caterer, food handling checks, allergy information

blocks.p: Use these risks to decide **which are worth paying for**, such as insurance or a larger deposit.

blocks.h: Health and safety on the day

ul: Check **fire exits** are clear and signed. If a fire exit is blocked by stacked exhibition boxes, have the boxes moved at once.
Know the **safe capacity** of each room, rated by the venue and fire authority. Do not exceed it.
Have a first-aid kit, a trained first-aider, a named person for emergencies, and phone numbers for hospital, police and fire.
Brief all staff and volunteers on the emergency plan and the assembly point.
Keep walkways clear of cables, bags and boxes.
Be ready for security needs at big events.
**Public liability** covers injury or damage to others.
**Event cancellation insurance** can cover losses if events beyond your control, such as a serious storm or the death or illness of a key person, force cancellation.
Read what the policy **covers and excludes** (for example storms already named when the policy was bought), the notice conditions and the claim steps. Insurers need records and dates.

blocks.note: A hurricane risk needs a decision date. Agree with the venue and the committee when you will decide to go ahead, change the date or move online, and how delegates will be told.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Reduce the conference's footprint: an event app instead of printing, water stations instead of plastic bottles, local suppliers, and reuse of signs and badges.

sections.title: Running the conference and following up

blocks.p: The **run sheet** is the minute-by-minute plan for the day, for the team, showing times, what happens, where, who is responsible, and equipment needed. It is **not** the same as the delegates' programme. Give copies to all team members and keep a master.

flow: Arrive early and walk the venue with the venue's events manager
Check rooms, layouts, signs, audio-visual equipment, catering times, fire exits and access
Hold a short briefing with staff and volunteers: tasks, timing, contacts, emergencies
Open registration before the first session, with pre-registered and on-the-door lanes
Keep to time: chairs signal time, the manager watches the clock
Keep an **incident log**: what happened, when, action, who
Check rooms, catering and delegate needs between sessions
Close: thank delegates, collect feedback, lock up, count equipment and cash

head: Incident
Immediate response
rows: Open extra lanes (such as one for pre-paid delegates); bring in a volunteer to direct; keep the first session short of late arrivals
Call the technician; load the backup copy of the slides on the conference computer; keep the speaker calm
Chair fills with a short discussion, a panel or a break; switch sessions if possible
Follow the plan: stop the session, lead people out by the nearest exit, assembly point, head count, do not re-enter
First-aider and emergency number; give space; log it
Tell the venue and the delegates; adjust the break; keep a small reserve

blocks.note: When something goes wrong, stay calm, decide quickly, tell the people affected and write it in the log. The audience judges you by how you respond.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Judge the conference **against the aims** set at the start. Collect:

ul: a **delegate survey**, sent on the last day or by text while the event is fresh (content, speakers, venue, catering, value, comments)
numbers: attendance, no-shows, income, costs
feedback from speakers, sponsors, exhibitors, staff and volunteers
incident log and the venue's report

blocks.p: **Response rate** = replies ÷ delegates asked. If 224 of 320 delegates reply, the response rate is 224 ÷ 320 = 70%. If 196 of those replies rate the event 4 or 5 out of 5, **87.5%** are satisfied (196 ÷ 224).

flow: Check every invoice against the quote and contract
Pay suppliers on time
Collect any money owed (sponsors, exhibitors)
Compare **actual with the budget** line by line and explain differences
Report the surplus or loss to the committee

blocks.p: **Example:** budgeted surplus J$150,000. Actual income J$6,400,000, actual costs J$6,100,000, so the actual surplus is J$300,000, which is J$150,000 above budget.

ul: Aims and results; attendance and numbers
Finance: budget against actual
Survey results and key comments
What worked and what did not (**lessons learned**), with actions, owners and dates for the next conference
Thanks to people
Recommendations

blocks.p: Follow up with delegates: **thank them, send slides or proceedings, and share agreed actions**. Record lessons so the next conference **repeats what worked and fixes the rest**.

blocks.note: Keep a folder of contracts, quotes, minutes, run sheets, risk register, survey results and the final report. The next team will thank you.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: explain what makes an event a conference and agree measurable aims
set up a steering committee and sub-committees with terms of reference and a timeline
list fixed and variable costs, work out break-even and the delegate fee, and set a contingency
evaluate a sponsorship offer for fit and conflicts of interest
compare venues, plan a site inspection and choose a room layout
check a venue contract for dates, rooms, price, attrition, guarantee, cancellation and force majeure
work out rooms owed under an attrition clause and meals under a catering guarantee
design a programme with plenary, breakout and networking, and brief speakers and chairs
plan registration, catering, transport, accessibility and volunteers, and protect delegates' data
build a risk register and plan for hurricanes, fire, capacity and insurance
use a run sheet and respond to incidents on the day
evaluate against the aims, close the finances and write a lessons-learned report

terms: Delegate
A person who attends a conference.
MICE
Meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions: the business-events part of tourism.
Plenary / keynote / breakout
A session for all; the main speaker; a smaller choice session.
Terms of reference
The written tasks, limits and reporting line of a committee.
Fixed / variable cost
A cost that does not change with delegates / one that rises with each delegate.
Break-even
The number of delegates at which income equals costs.
Contingency
Money held back for the unforeseen.
Early-bird rate
A reduced fee for early payment.
Room block / attrition
Rooms held for delegates / the percentage you may release without penalty.
Guarantee
The final number of meals you must pay for.
Force majeure
A clause freeing both sides after events beyond their control.
Site inspection
A visit to check a venue before booking.
Run sheet
The minute-by-minute plan for the day.
No-show
A registered delegate who neither attends nor cancels.
Hybrid
A conference with some delegates in the room and some online.
Stand
The space an exhibitor pays for.

c1.title: Early-childhood educators' conference
c1.text: A national association of early-childhood educators plans a two-day conference in Mandeville for about 120 delegates. Fixed costs are J$1,800,000 (venue, sound, speakers, marketing and insurance). Each delegate costs J$6,000 in meals and materials. The planned fee is J$20,000. A sponsor has offered J$600,000. The treasurer, Mrs Lorna Clarke, wants a 10% contingency on total costs at 120 delegates.

c2.title: Hotel contract for a trade conference
c2.text: A trade association books 60 rooms for three nights at J$16,000 a night for out-of-town delegates. The hotel contract allows the group to take 15% fewer rooms than the block without charge, and the group ends up using 45 rooms. The contract also says the final number of lunches must be given 72 hours before the event (the guarantee). The association guaranteed 180 lunches at J$3,500 each, and only 165 delegates attended. During the site inspection, the organiser noticed that two pillars in the ballroom block the view from some seats.

c3.title: Agribusiness conference programme
c3.text: An agribusiness association is planning a two-day conference for 200 delegates. Three breakout sessions will run at once in rooms that each hold 60 people. The keynote speaker is flying in from Trinidad. Two days before the conference, one of the other main speakers withdraws. Last year, a speaker overran by 25 minutes and the lunch was delayed. Several delegates also had trouble opening their slides on the venue's computer.

c4.title: October conference at a St Ann resort
c4.text: A professional association is holding a three-day residential conference at a resort in Runaway Bay, St Ann, in early October, with 300 delegates. The risk officer, Mr Dwayne Campbell, is building the risk register. A hurricane near the date would be very damaging. The committee is thinking of buying event cancellation insurance. A delegate who has a hearing impairment has registered, and the venue's main hall has two fire exits at the back.

c5.title: Conference evaluation and closing
c5.text: A conference for 320 delegates has ended. The evaluation survey was sent to all delegates and 224 replied, of whom 196 rated the event 4 or 5 out of 5. Many comments said that the Day 2 lunch queue was too long. The budgeted surplus was J$150,000. Actual income was J$6,400,000 and actual costs were J$6,100,000. The conference manager, Ms Carol Francis, must now close the finances and write the final report.

questions.q: How many paying delegates are needed to break even, before the sponsor's money is counted?
questions.why: Contribution per delegate = 20,000 − 6,000 = J$14,000. 1,800,000 ÷ 14,000 = 128.57, which must be rounded up to 129 delegates, because 128 would leave a small loss.

questions.q: If the sponsor's J$600,000 is used to cover part of the fixed costs, how many paying delegates are needed to break even?
questions.why: Fixed costs left to cover = 1,800,000 − 600,000 = J$1,200,000. 1,200,000 ÷ 14,000 = 85.7, rounded up to 86 delegates.

questions.q: What contingency should Mrs Clarke hold at 120 delegates?
questions.why: Total costs at 120 delegates = 1,800,000 + (120 × 6,000) = 1,800,000 + 720,000 = J$2,520,000. 10% of that is J$252,000. A common slip is to take 10% of the fixed costs only (J$180,000).

questions.q: Before accepting the J$600,000 sponsorship, what should the committee do?
o: Accept at once, since the money lowers the fee for every delegate who registers
Ask the sponsor to choose the speakers and the programme, since it is paying for them
Check fit with the aims, agree the benefits in writing and look for conflicts
Accept it and promise the sponsor a free stand at every conference in the next five years
questions.why: Sponsorship needs checking: does the sponsor fit the aims, what exactly does it get, and does it have any conflict with the association or its members. Agree it in writing.

questions.q: Under the attrition clause, how much does the group owe for unused rooms?
questions.why: 15% of 60 = 9, so the minimum is 51 rooms. The group used 45, which is 6 short. 6 rooms × 3 nights × J$16,000 = J$288,000.

questions.q: What does the association owe for lunches under the guarantee, at J$3,500 each?
questions.why: The association must pay for the guaranteed 180 lunches, even though 165 attended: 180 × 3,500 = J$630,000. It cannot pay for the number who came.

questions.q: The site inspection shows that two ballroom pillars block some views. What is the best step?
o: Raise it in writing before signing, and ask for another room or layout with the capacity in the contract
Sign the contract and ask delegates to arrive early to take the seats that have a good view
Take no action, since the hotel has promised in conversation that the room will hold 200 delegates
Tell delegates in the printed programme that some seats have a restricted view of the stage
questions.why: Faults found at the inspection should be solved before signing. Ask for a better room or layout, and get the promised capacity and layout in writing. Verbal promises do not protect the association.

questions.q: Which clause would cover the association if a hurricane forced the hotel to close its ballroom the week before the conference?
o: Attrition, which lets the group take fewer rooms than the block without paying for them
The catering guarantee, which fixes the final number of lunches the group must pay for
The payment clause, which sets the dates and amounts of each deposit to the hotel
Force majeure, which frees both sides after events outside their control
questions.why: Force majeure covers events outside both parties' control, such as a hurricane. Attrition and guarantee deal with room and meal numbers; payment deals with deposits.

questions.q: Three breakout sessions run at once in rooms that each hold 60, for 200 delegates. How should the organiser avoid overcrowding?
o: Let delegates choose on the day and ask those who cannot find a seat to stand at the back
Put the most popular topic in a room for 60 and hope that some delegates go elsewhere
Tell delegates to attend the session that matches their job title, whatever they prefer
Ask delegates to choose at registration, set a limit for each session and keep a reserve list
questions.why: Choosing in advance, with limits, lets the team plan rooms and handouts and avoids an unsafe overcrowded room. Standing at the back is unsafe and lowers the quality of the session.

questions.q: One main speaker withdraws two days before the conference. Which preparation would best have reduced the problem?
o: A note in the printed programme that all speakers and times may change
A refund offered to every delegate who registered to hear that speaker
A named back-up speaker, or a panel prepared in advance for key slots
A second keynote speaker invited for each of the other main slots
questions.why: Speakers are a known risk. A back-up speaker or a panel can fill the slot, and the chair can adjust. Planned in advance, this keeps the programme to time.

questions.q: Last year a speaker overran by 25 minutes and the lunch was delayed. What is the best control this year?
o: Remove the lunch break so that speakers can use all the time that they need
Give chairs a written brief and a way to signal time, and keep to the schedule
Ask speakers to speak for no more than five minutes, whatever their topic may be
Let the venue's catering staff decide when lunch is served each day
questions.why: A chair with a written brief and agreed time signals can keep sessions to time, so that later speakers and breaks are not squeezed. Overrunning is a planning matter, not only a speaker's fault.

questions.q: Delegates had trouble opening slides on the venue's computer. What is the best way to avoid this?
o: Collect slides early, load them on one computer and hold a technical rehearsal the day before
Ask each speaker to bring a laptop and connect it at the start of his or her own session
Ask every speaker to talk without slides, so that no technical problem can occur
Leave it to the venue's staff, who know the equipment and will fix any problem quickly
questions.why: Collected slides, one computer and a rehearsal with the technician find problems in advance. Also keep a backup copy of the slides on a drive.

questions.q: Mr Campbell scores a hurricane near the date as likelihood 4 and impact 5. How should it be treated?
o: As a top-priority risk with a named owner, a decision date and controls
As a low risk, since a hurricane is unlikely during any one week
As a risk that needs no action, since nobody can control the weather
As a risk to be noted once the conference programme is final
questions.why: 4 × 5 = 20, a high score. You cannot stop a hurricane, but you can control the response: decision date, communication plan, agreements with the venue and insurer, and online back-up.

questions.q: Before buying event cancellation insurance, what should the committee do?
o: Buy the cheapest cover so that the budget is protected
Buy cover and tell the insurer about any hurricane warning only after the event is cancelled
Assume that it covers all causes of cancellation
Read what the policy covers and excludes, the notice conditions and the claim steps
questions.why: Policies differ in what they cover and exclude (for example storms already named at purchase), and in notice and claim conditions. Read before buying, and keep records.

questions.q: How should the organisers respond to the delegate with a hearing impairment?
o: Ask the delegate to bring a friend to help, to save the cost of any special arrangements
Send the delegate the slides after the conference instead of arranging anything in the hall
Ask what support is needed and arrange, for example, an interpreter or hearing loop and front seating
Treat the delegate like every other delegate and arrange nothing that is special
questions.why: Ask the delegate what helps, then plan it in advance: an interpreter, hearing loop, front seating and captions. Good planning means the delegate can take part fully.

questions.q: During setup, boxes for the exhibition are stacked in front of one of the two fire exits at the back of the hall. What should the conference manager do?
o: Leave them until the next break, since the other exit at the back is clear
Have them moved at once and keep both exits clear and unlocked all through the event
Cover the boxes with a cloth so that the exit sign can still be seen over them
Ask delegates to use the front doors instead of the exits at the back
questions.why: Blocked exits can cost lives in an emergency. Move the boxes immediately and make sure exits stay clear, marked and unlocked throughout.

questions.q: What was the response rate to the survey?
questions.why: 224 ÷ 320 = 0.70 = 70%. The response rate is the replies as a share of those asked (delegates), not of those who replied.

questions.q: What share of respondents were satisfied (rated 4 or 5)?
questions.why: 196 ÷ 224 = 0.875 = 87.5%. The base is the number of replies (224). 61.3% would be 196 ÷ 320, which is the share of all delegates.

questions.q: How did the conference perform against the budgeted surplus?
o: The actual surplus of J$300,000 was J$150,000 below the budgeted surplus of the conference
The surplus of J$150,000 matched the budgeted surplus of J$150,000 exactly
There was a loss of J$300,000 for the whole conference, because costs were above budget
The actual surplus of J$300,000 was J$150,000 above budget
questions.why: Actual surplus = 6,400,000 − 6,100,000 = J$300,000, against J$150,000 budgeted. That is J$150,000 above budget. Then explain the difference line by line in the report.

questions.q: Many comments said that the Day 2 lunch queue was too long. What should Ms Francis do with this?
o: Ignore it, because one comment about one meal does not matter much
Remove lunch from the next conference altogether to avoid long queues
Record it in the lessons-learned report, with an action, an owner and a date
Reply to each comment with a full explanation of why the queue was long
questions.why: Evaluation is useful only if it leads to action. Record the finding and agree a specific improvement, such as more serving points or staggered lunch times, with an owner and date.
